screens.title: Ethereum Blockchain Architecture and Components
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll see what makes Ethereum different from earlier blockchains, and why that difference matters for building dApps. Ethereum uses an account-based model rather than UTXOs, so the network maintains a single global world state that maps addresses to account objects, balances, and contract data. The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the deterministic runtime that executes smart contract code and ensures every node reaches the same state after processing the same transactions. We will unpack the anatomy of a block: header fields like the parent hash, timestamp, and the key Merkle roots that cryptographically summarize transactions, state, and receipts. You will also learn the difference between Externally Owned Accounts and Contract Accounts, how storage and code are represented, and the common interaction patterns you need to avoid mistakes like sending Ether to a contract that cannot accept it. By the end of the chapter, you will be able to read block metadata with web3. js, reason about how a state root proves the network state, and appreciate how deterministic execution underpins consensus. Keep an eye out for the hands-on example that walks through a small web3. js script to fetch a block and inspect its header and first transaction.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Overview
Ethereum Blockchain Architecture and Components
Learn how the EVM, account-based model, blocks, and the world state work together to power decentralized applications.
In this lesson

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives frame the core knowledge and practical skills you will build. First, you will distinguish Ethereum from other blockchains by understanding the account-based model versus the UTXO model; we will give an example contrast with Bitcoin so you can see why state is stored differently. Second, you will explain what the Ethereum Virtual Machine does: a deterministic runtime that executes smart contract bytecode and produces identical state transitions on every node. Third, you will describe what makes up an Ethereum block, including header fields such as the parent hash, timestamp, and the three Merkle roots for transactions, state, and receipts; you'll learn how those roots allow compact integrity checks. Finally, you will understand Ethereum's world state and its account objects, including the nonce, balance, storageRoot, and codeHash fields, so you can interpret how a transfer or contract call mutates state. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you know when you can apply the knowledge to read blocks with web3. js and reason about contract interactions.

screens.title: Account-Based Model vs UTXO (High-Level)
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear contrast. Bitcoin uses UTXOs: each transaction consumes outputs and produces new outputs. Ethereum instead maintains an account-based world state — a mapping from addresses to account objects that include a nonce and balance and, for contracts, storage and code. That difference is significant. When you transfer Ether, Ethereum directly updates account balances in the world state; there is no need to track which coin-chunk was spent. This makes contract interactions and persistent storage straightforward, because contract state lives at an address and is updated in-place. A concrete example: sending Ether from one account to another updates two balances and the sender's nonce; the state root in the resulting block will reflect those new values. A common misconception is to think account-based systems are simpler for privacy — they are not; they centralize state and make tracing funds through account balances different from tracing discrete UTXOs. Another misconception is that account-based models eliminate the need for cryptographic proofs — they don't. Merkle roots still cryptographically summarize state and enable proofs of inclusion or correctness. Key takeaway: the account model makes persistent contract storage and direct balance updates natural, and it is the reason Ethereum can act as a global computer where contracts hold state and code at addresses. How does this change the way you design a dApp's data model?

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: The account model enables persistent contract storage and simpler in-place updates, which is central to how dApps manage state and logic on Ethereum.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Account Model Comparison
Ethereum (Account-based)
State is a global mapping of addresses to account objects
  • Account object contains nonce and balance; contracts also have storageRoot and codeHash.
  • Transfers update balances directly and change the world state.
  • Ideal for persistent contract storage and stateful dApps.
Concrete example
Alice sends 1 Ether to Bob: Alice.balance decreases, Bob.balance increases, Alice.nonce increments, and the stateRoot changes to reflect the new world state.
Bitcoin (UTXO) — quick contrast
Transactions consume outputs and create new outputs
  • State is implicit through unspent outputs rather than a single global mapping.
  • Tracing funds follows outputs; updates are handled by spending and creating outputs.
  • Good for simple currency transfer semantics but more awkward for persistent contracts.
Misconception
People assume account models always simplify privacy or scaling. In practice, they change how you reason about ownership and state, but privacy and scaling are separate trade-offs.
Key takeaway
Account model is the foundation for contract state and the EVM’s in-place updates.
Try this
When designing data for a dApp, map entities to accounts or contract storage rather than UTXO outputs.
Check
Can a state change be represented as a direct update to an account object? If yes, account model fits well.

screens.title: Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
screens.narratorSegment: Define the EVM clearly: it is the deterministic state machine that executes smart contract bytecode and produces the state transitions every node must agree on. Deterministic means that given the same starting state and the same ordered transactions, every node that runs the EVM arrives at the same resulting world state. The EVM is quasi-Turing complete: it can express general computation within practical limits on execution. It is sandboxed so contracts cannot access a node's file system, direct network calls, or other external resources; this reduces attack surface and ensures predictable execution. For example, when a user calls a token contract function, the EVM executes the contract code instructions and updates storage and balances; the changes are captured in the resulting stateRoot of the block. A common misconception is to treat the EVM as a single physical C P U; instead, think of it as a virtual C P U that every node runs independently to simulate the same computation. Concrete takeaway: every smart contract you write will be compiled to bytecode that the EVM executes deterministically, so code correctness and understanding side effects are critical. Question to reflect on: how does sandboxing influence how you design external integrations for a dApp?

keyIdea.title: EVM summary
keyIdea.text: The EVM deterministically executes contract bytecode in a sandbox so that all nodes reach the same world state after applying the same transactions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Ethereum Virtual Machine
What is the EVM?
A deterministic runtime that executes compiled smart contract bytecode on every node. It simulates a virtual CPU and applies state changes that become part of the world state.
Properties
  • Deterministic execution
  • Sandboxed environment
  • Executes contract bytecode (Solidity/Vyper)
Implication
Correctness matters: the EVM enforces that code behaves the same everywhere, so bugs cause identical effects across the network.
Analogy
Think of the EVM as a virtual CPU each node runs to process the same program instructions and arrive at the same result.
Example
A token transfer call executes code that adjusts storage values and emits events; the EVM runs that code and the resulting storage changes become part of the new world state.
Misconception
The EVM is not one physical CPU — it's the same virtual machine simulated by every node, which is why identical inputs produce identical state transitions.
Key Takeaway

Design contracts mindful of deterministic execution and sandboxing so behavior is predictable and secure across nodes.

screens.title: Ethereum Block Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A block is the atomic unit that carries validated transactions and the metadata nodes use to link and verify chain history. At the top is the block header: it contains the block number, timestamp, parent hash that links to the previous block, and the Merkle roots: transactionsRoot, stateRoot, and receiptsRoot. TransactionsRoot is a Merkle root summarizing all transactions included in the block; it enables compact proofs that a transaction is part of a block. StateRoot is the hash representing the entire world state after processing all block transactions. ReceiptsRoot summarizes execution receipts such as logs and status. The header also includes fields like gasUsed and gasLimit that describe resources consumed and allowed in the block. Example: after applying all transactions in a block, nodes compute a new stateRoot; by comparing stateRoot values across nodes, the network can verify that they reached the same world state. A common mistake is focusing only on transaction hashes; the stateRoot is the authoritative snapshot of the world. Key takeaway: the header ties together chain history, transaction inclusion proofs, and the authoritative post-block state, allowing nodes and light clients to verify consistency without keeping full data.

keyIdea.title: Header role
keyIdea.text: Block headers link history and compactly summarize transactions and post-block state using Merkle roots, enabling verification across nodes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Block Structure
Block header: the summary that links blocks
Key header fields cryptographically summarize block contents and anchor the chain through parent hash references.
Parent Hash
Links this block to its predecessor and ensures chain continuity.
Transactions Root
Merkle root summarizing all transactions included in the block.
State Root
Hash of the entire world state after processing block transactions — the authoritative snapshot.
Receipts Root
Summarizes execution receipts, logs, and statuses for included transactions.
Gas fields
gasUsed and gasLimit report resources consumed and allowed for the block.
Concrete scenario
A block contains multiple transactions. Nodes compute transactionsRoot, apply each transaction to update state, and then compute the final stateRoot. Consensus requires matching stateRoot values across nodes.
Common mistake
Focusing only on transaction hashes without checking the stateRoot can miss inconsistencies in post-transaction state across nodes.
Key Takeaway

Block headers cryptographically tie together chain history and the authoritative post-block world state through Merkle roots.

screens.title: Merkle Trees and Roots
screens.narratorSegment: Merkle trees let Ethereum summarize large collections of data—transactions, receipts, or state nodes—with a single cryptographic root. Each leaf in a Merkle tree is a hash of a data item; parent nodes hash the concatenation of their children, and the top hash is the Merkle root. This structure allows a compact proof that a particular item is included in the set: you only need the chain of sibling hashes from the leaf to the root. In Ethereum blocks, the transactionsRoot is a Merkle root of all transactions, allowing a light client or external verifier to confirm inclusion without downloading every transaction. The stateRoot is conceptually similar but summarizes the entire world state. For example, to prove that a specific account balance exists at a block height, a verifier can use a Merkle proof against the stateRoot rather than trusting a snapshot. A common misconception is that Merkle roots themselves reveal data; they do not. A root is a commitment to underlying content but does not expose content without the proper proof values. Takeaway: Merkle trees enable efficient, auditable proofs of inclusion that scale verification and let clients rely on compact cryptographic summaries instead of full datasets. How might you use inclusion proofs in a dApp that needs to verify off-chain assertions?

keyIdea.title: Merkle root utility
keyIdea.text: Merkle roots enable compact proofs of inclusion so verifiers can confirm specific data without the entire dataset.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Merkle Trees
How Merkle trees work
Hash leaves, pairwise combine and hash upward until one top-level root stands as a compact commitment to all leaves.
Leaf: hash(transaction)
Parent: hash(childA || childB)
Root: top-level hash representing entire set
Inclusion proof
A verifier needs only sibling hashes along the path from a leaf to the root to confirm inclusion against the known root.
Applications
  • transactionsRoot: proves a transaction is included in a block
  • stateRoot: commits to the post-block world state
  • receiptsRoot: summarizes execution receipts and logs
Misconception
A Merkle root does not reveal the underlying data. It only commits to it; proofs or the full data are required to reconstruct content.
Key Takeaway

Merkle trees let you verify inclusion efficiently, making light clients and proofs possible without full data downloads.

screens.title: World State and Account Object
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum's world state is the canonical mapping of addresses to account objects. Each account object has four fields you must know: nonce, balance, storageRoot, and codeHash. Nonce is a counter: for Externally Owned Accounts it counts outgoing transactions, and for contracts it may represent creation counts. Balance is the amount of Ether held. storageRoot is a Merkle root summarizing a contract's persistent storage slots; it is meaningful only for contract accounts. codeHash is the hash of the contract's EVM code and is empty for EOAs. The world state evolves as blocks arrive: when transactions execute, nodes apply the specified state changes to account objects and compute a new stateRoot that appears in the block header. Example: a token contract that updates a mapping of balances will modify the contract's storage slots; the storageRoot changes and that update is reflected in the global stateRoot once the block is finalized. Misconception to avoid: treating account fields as independent snapshots; they are interdependent — a transaction may change multiple account fields atomically. Key takeaway: understanding these four fields lets you reason about what changes when a transaction runs and how those changes are committed into the blockchain.

keyIdea.title: Account fields
keyIdea.text: nonce, balance, storageRoot, and codeHash form the account object; transactions mutate these fields and the stateRoot reflects their aggregated change.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › World State & Accounts
Account object — four essential fields
Nonce
Transaction counter for EOAs; ensures uniqueness and prevents replay.
Balance
Amount of Ether held by the account.
storageRoot
Merkle root summarizing a contract's persistent storage slots; relevant for contract accounts only.
codeHash
Hash of the account's EVM code; empty for externally controlled accounts.
How state evolves
Nodes apply transactions in order, update account fields, and compute the new stateRoot that appears in the block header to commit the new world state.
Example
A contract writes a new value to storage; that changes its storageRoot, which contributes to a different stateRoot once the block finalizes.
Misconception
Do not assume codeHash changes when storage changes — codeHash only changes when the contract code itself is updated.
Key Takeaway

Account fields together define on-chain identity and persistent state; track them to reason about transaction effects.

screens.title: Externally Owned Accounts vs Contract Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum exposes two primary account types with distinct roles. Externally Owned Accounts, or EOAs, are controlled by private keys. They have a nonce and a balance and can initiate transactions: sending Ether or invoking contract functions. By contrast, Contract Accounts are controlled by EVM bytecode deployed at an address. They have a balance and persistent storage, but they cannot initiate transactions on their own — they only run code when called by an EOA or another contract. A concrete example: when you use a wallet to press 'send', your EOA creates and signs a transaction; that transaction triggers the EVM to execute the target contract's code if the recipient is a contract account. A common beginner mistake is sending Ether to a contract without checking whether it can accept plain transfers. If the contract lacks a payable fallback or specific function to receive Ether, funds may be effectively locked. Always inspect contract interfaces before transferring Ether. Takeaway: design interactions so EOAs initiate and contracts encode predictable responses; this mental model helps you avoid stuck funds and reasoning errors about who can trigger on-chain actions.

keyIdea.title: Roles clarified
keyIdea.text: EOAs hold keys and initiate transactions; contract accounts hold code and storage and only act when executed by transactions or calls.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Account Types
Externally Owned Account (EOA)
Controlled by a private key, can sign and send transactions, has nonce and balance but no code or storage.
Example
A MetaMask wallet creates a signed transaction from your EOA to call a contract function or send Ether.
Contract Account
Controlled by code deployed at the address, can hold balance and storage, but only executes when called.
Pitfall
Sending Ether directly to a contract without a payable fallback may lock funds. Always confirm the contract accepts direct transfers.
Check your understanding
Who creates and signs transactions? Who executes code in response?
Pro tip
Inspect contract ABI and fallback functions before sending native Ether transfers.
Key Takeaway
EOAs initiate; contracts respond. This separation defines how on-chain interactions flow.

screens.title: Hands-on: Exploring Blocks with web3.js
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough takes the web3. js example from the chapter and explains what each step does and why it matters. First you create a Web3 instance pointed at a provider such as Infura or Alchemy; this lets your script query the Ethereum node's JSON-RPC endpoints. Then you request the latest block number, and finally fetch the full block with the second argument set to true so transactions are returned as objects rather than hashes. Inspect fields printed by the script: block. hash and parentHash link the block into the chain; timestamp shows when the block was produced; miner identifies the coinbase address; gasUsed and gasLimit report resource usage; transactionsRoot, stateRoot, and receiptsRoot are Merkle roots you can compare to validate inclusion. When reading a transaction object, note from, to, value, gas, gasPrice, and input data. A concrete example: running the script prints the latest block header and the first transaction details, letting you observe stateRoot and transactionsRoot values in practice. Misconception check: the script output is observational — it does not change on-chain state. Use this pattern to verify and diagnose blocks and transactions before building higher-level application logic.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › web3.js Block Explorer
Code template
const Web3 = require('web3');

// Replace with your Infura project ID
const INFURA_PROJECT_ID = 'YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID';
const providerUrl = `https://mainnet.infura.io/v3/${INFURA_PROJECT_ID}`;
const web3 = new Web3(providerUrl);

async function exploreBlock() {
  try {
    const latestBlockNumber = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
    console.log(`Latest Block Number: ${latestBlockNumber}`);

    const latestBlock = await web3.eth.getBlock(latestBlockNumber, true);
    console.log('Block Hash:', latestBlock.hash);
    console.log('Parent Hash:', latestBlock.parentHash);
    console.log('Timestamp:', new Date(latestBlock.timestamp * 1000).toUTCString());
    console.log('Gas Used:', latestBlock.gasUsed);
    console.log('Transactions Root:', latestBlock.transactionsRoot);
    console.log('State Root:', latestBlock.stateRoot);

    if (latestBlock.transactions.length > 0) {
      const firstTx = latestBlock.transactions[0];
      console.log('First Tx Hash:', firstTx.hash);
      console.log('From:', firstTx.from);
      console.log('To:', firstTx.to);
      console.log('Value (Wei):', firstTx.value);
    }
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error exploring block:', error);
  }
}

exploreBlock();
This exact template prints header fields and a sample transaction so you can map printed roots back to theory discussed earlier in the chapter.
What to observe
  • stateRoot: the authoritative post-block world state hash.
  • transactionsRoot: proves inclusion of any transaction in the block.
  • first transaction fields: from, to, value, input; useful for debugging.
Misconception
Running the script reads state; it doesn't alter the chain. To change on-chain state you must sign and broadcast transactions from an EOA.
Key Takeaway

Use web3.js to connect theory to live data — inspecting headers and transactions solidifies understanding of state commitments.

screens.title: From Transaction to New StateRoot
screens.narratorSegment: Trace the life of a transaction to see how the world state changes. Step one: an EOA creates and signs a transaction and broadcasts it to the network. Step two: miners or validators include that transaction in a block proposal. Step three: all full nodes execute the transaction using the EVM, applying code logic if the recipient is a contract and updating account fields such as nonces, balances, or storage. Step four: after processing every transaction in the block, nodes compute the new stateRoot that summarizes the updated world state. For example, a token transfer will adjust balances stored in contract storage; these storage slot changes alter storageRoots and ultimately the stateRoot. A frequent misconception is treating transactions as isolated changes; in fact, they are sequential and can interact because later transactions observe earlier state changes within the same block. Practical implication: transaction ordering matters, and deterministic EVM execution ensures that every node processing the same ordered transactions arrives at the same stateRoot. Key takeaway: a transaction is the unit of change, the EVM applies it, and the stateRoot is the cryptographic fingerprint of the new world state.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Transaction → State
Sequential steps
1. Create & sign
An EOA creates and signs a transaction to transfer value or call a contract function.
2. Inclusion in a block
Validators include the transaction in a block; ordering matters for subsequent state changes.
3. EVM execution
Every node executes the transaction deterministically, applying any contract code and updating accounts.
4. Compute stateRoot
After processing all block transactions, nodes compute the new stateRoot that commits the updated world state.
Concrete example
Two transactions in the same block can interact: the second may rely on storage written by the first. Order determines the resulting stateRoot.
Misconception
Assuming transactions are independent within a block is unsafe; they execute in sequence and can affect each other.
Key Takeaway

Transaction ordering plus deterministic EVM execution produces the single stateRoot that nodes use to verify the new world state.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll see what makes Ethereum different from earlier blockchains, and why that difference matters for building dApps. Ethereum uses an account-based model rather than UTXOs, so the network maintains a single global world state that maps addresses to account objects, balances, and contract data. The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the deterministic runtime that executes smart contract code and ensures every node reaches the same state after processing the same transactions. We will unpack the anatomy of a block: header fields like the parent hash, timestamp, and the key Merkle roots that cryptographically summarize transactions, state, and receipts. You will also learn the difference between Externally Owned Accounts and Contract Accounts, how storage and code are represented, and the common interaction patterns you need to avoid mistakes like sending Ether to a contract that cannot accept it. By the end of the chapter, you will be able to read block metadata with web3. js, reason about how a state root proves the network state, and appreciate how deterministic execution underpins consensus. Keep an eye out for the hands-on example that walks through a small web3. js script to fetch a block and inspect its header and first transaction.

These objectives frame the core knowledge and practical skills you will build. First, you will distinguish Ethereum from other blockchains by understanding the account-based model versus the UTXO model; we will give an example contrast with Bitcoin so you can see why state is stored differently. Second, you will explain what the Ethereum Virtual Machine does: a deterministic runtime that executes smart contract bytecode and produces identical state transitions on every node. Third, you will describe what makes up an Ethereum block, including header fields such as the parent hash, timestamp, and the three Merkle roots for transactions, state, and receipts; you'll learn how those roots allow compact integrity checks. Finally, you will understand Ethereum's world state and its account objects, including the nonce, balance, storageRoot, and codeHash fields, so you can interpret how a transfer or contract call mutates state. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you know when you can apply the knowledge to read blocks with web3. js and reason about contract interactions.

These additional objectives focus on applying your understanding. You will identify the two primary Ethereum account types — Externally Owned Accounts and Contract Accounts — and explain who or what controls each. You will run a small web3. js script to fetch the latest block and inspect header fields such as transactionsRoot, stateRoot, and receiptsRoot so you can see how a block summarizes its contents. You will also learn to read a transaction object returned by web3. js, noting fields like from, to, value, gas, and input data so you can interpret what a transaction actually did on-chain. Finally, you will practice a common troubleshooting check: when Ether appears to be “stuck” at a contract address, learn to verify whether the contract has a payable fallback or handles direct transfers. Each objective links concept to concrete steps so you can verify state changes on a real node and reason about contract interactions with confidence.

Start with a clear contrast. Bitcoin uses UTXOs: each transaction consumes outputs and produces new outputs. Ethereum instead maintains an account-based world state — a mapping from addresses to account objects that include a nonce and balance and, for contracts, storage and code. That difference is significant. When you transfer Ether, Ethereum directly updates account balances in the world state; there is no need to track which coin-chunk was spent. This makes contract interactions and persistent storage straightforward, because contract state lives at an address and is updated in-place. A concrete example: sending Ether from one account to another updates two balances and the sender's nonce; the state root in the resulting block will reflect those new values. A common misconception is to think account-based systems are simpler for privacy — they are not; they centralize state and make tracing funds through account balances different from tracing discrete UTXOs. Another misconception is that account-based models eliminate the need for cryptographic proofs — they don't. Merkle roots still cryptographically summarize state and enable proofs of inclusion or correctness. Key takeaway: the account model makes persistent contract storage and direct balance updates natural, and it is the reason Ethereum can act as a global computer where contracts hold state and code at addresses. How does this change the way you design a dApp's data model?

Define the EVM clearly: it is the deterministic state machine that executes smart contract bytecode and produces the state transitions every node must agree on. Deterministic means that given the same starting state and the same ordered transactions, every node that runs the EVM arrives at the same resulting world state. The EVM is quasi-Turing complete: it can express general computation within practical limits on execution. It is sandboxed so contracts cannot access a node's file system, direct network calls, or other external resources; this reduces attack surface and ensures predictable execution. For example, when a user calls a token contract function, the EVM executes the contract code instructions and updates storage and balances; the changes are captured in the resulting stateRoot of the block. A common misconception is to treat the EVM as a single physical C P U; instead, think of it as a virtual C P U that every node runs independently to simulate the same computation. Concrete takeaway: every smart contract you write will be compiled to bytecode that the EVM executes deterministically, so code correctness and understanding side effects are critical. Question to reflect on: how does sandboxing influence how you design external integrations for a dApp?

A block is the atomic unit that carries validated transactions and the metadata nodes use to link and verify chain history. At the top is the block header: it contains the block number, timestamp, parent hash that links to the previous block, and the Merkle roots: transactionsRoot, stateRoot, and receiptsRoot. TransactionsRoot is a Merkle root summarizing all transactions included in the block; it enables compact proofs that a transaction is part of a block. StateRoot is the hash representing the entire world state after processing all block transactions. ReceiptsRoot summarizes execution receipts such as logs and status. The header also includes fields like gasUsed and gasLimit that describe resources consumed and allowed in the block. Example: after applying all transactions in a block, nodes compute a new stateRoot; by comparing stateRoot values across nodes, the network can verify that they reached the same world state. A common mistake is focusing only on transaction hashes; the stateRoot is the authoritative snapshot of the world. Key takeaway: the header ties together chain history, transaction inclusion proofs, and the authoritative post-block state, allowing nodes and light clients to verify consistency without keeping full data.

Merkle trees let Ethereum summarize large collections of data—transactions, receipts, or state nodes—with a single cryptographic root. Each leaf in a Merkle tree is a hash of a data item; parent nodes hash the concatenation of their children, and the top hash is the Merkle root. This structure allows a compact proof that a particular item is included in the set: you only need the chain of sibling hashes from the leaf to the root. In Ethereum blocks, the transactionsRoot is a Merkle root of all transactions, allowing a light client or external verifier to confirm inclusion without downloading every transaction. The stateRoot is conceptually similar but summarizes the entire world state. For example, to prove that a specific account balance exists at a block height, a verifier can use a Merkle proof against the stateRoot rather than trusting a snapshot. A common misconception is that Merkle roots themselves reveal data; they do not. A root is a commitment to underlying content but does not expose content without the proper proof values. Takeaway: Merkle trees enable efficient, auditable proofs of inclusion that scale verification and let clients rely on compact cryptographic summaries instead of full datasets. How might you use inclusion proofs in a dApp that needs to verify off-chain assertions?

Ethereum's world state is the canonical mapping of addresses to account objects. Each account object has four fields you must know: nonce, balance, storageRoot, and codeHash. Nonce is a counter: for Externally Owned Accounts it counts outgoing transactions, and for contracts it may represent creation counts. Balance is the amount of Ether held. storageRoot is a Merkle root summarizing a contract's persistent storage slots; it is meaningful only for contract accounts. codeHash is the hash of the contract's EVM code and is empty for EOAs. The world state evolves as blocks arrive: when transactions execute, nodes apply the specified state changes to account objects and compute a new stateRoot that appears in the block header. Example: a token contract that updates a mapping of balances will modify the contract's storage slots; the storageRoot changes and that update is reflected in the global stateRoot once the block is finalized. Misconception to avoid: treating account fields as independent snapshots; they are interdependent — a transaction may change multiple account fields atomically. Key takeaway: understanding these four fields lets you reason about what changes when a transaction runs and how those changes are committed into the blockchain.

Ethereum exposes two primary account types with distinct roles. Externally Owned Accounts, or EOAs, are controlled by private keys. They have a nonce and a balance and can initiate transactions: sending Ether or invoking contract functions. By contrast, Contract Accounts are controlled by EVM bytecode deployed at an address. They have a balance and persistent storage, but they cannot initiate transactions on their own — they only run code when called by an EOA or another contract. A concrete example: when you use a wallet to press 'send', your EOA creates and signs a transaction; that transaction triggers the EVM to execute the target contract's code if the recipient is a contract account. A common beginner mistake is sending Ether to a contract without checking whether it can accept plain transfers. If the contract lacks a payable fallback or specific function to receive Ether, funds may be effectively locked. Always inspect contract interfaces before transferring Ether. Takeaway: design interactions so EOAs initiate and contracts encode predictable responses; this mental model helps you avoid stuck funds and reasoning errors about who can trigger on-chain actions.

This walkthrough takes the web3. js example from the chapter and explains what each step does and why it matters. First you create a Web3 instance pointed at a provider such as Infura or Alchemy; this lets your script query the Ethereum node's JSON-RPC endpoints. Then you request the latest block number, and finally fetch the full block with the second argument set to true so transactions are returned as objects rather than hashes. Inspect fields printed by the script: block. hash and parentHash link the block into the chain; timestamp shows when the block was produced; miner identifies the coinbase address; gasUsed and gasLimit report resource usage; transactionsRoot, stateRoot, and receiptsRoot are Merkle roots you can compare to validate inclusion. When reading a transaction object, note from, to, value, gas, gasPrice, and input data. A concrete example: running the script prints the latest block header and the first transaction details, letting you observe stateRoot and transactionsRoot values in practice. Misconception check: the script output is observational — it does not change on-chain state. Use this pattern to verify and diagnose blocks and transactions before building higher-level application logic.

Trace the life of a transaction to see how the world state changes. Step one: an EOA creates and signs a transaction and broadcasts it to the network. Step two: miners or validators include that transaction in a block proposal. Step three: all full nodes execute the transaction using the EVM, applying code logic if the recipient is a contract and updating account fields such as nonces, balances, or storage. Step four: after processing every transaction in the block, nodes compute the new stateRoot that summarizes the updated world state. For example, a token transfer will adjust balances stored in contract storage; these storage slot changes alter storageRoots and ultimately the stateRoot. A frequent misconception is treating transactions as isolated changes; in fact, they are sequential and can interact because later transactions observe earlier state changes within the same block. Practical implication: transaction ordering matters, and deterministic EVM execution ensures that every node processing the same ordered transactions arrives at the same stateRoot. Key takeaway: a transaction is the unit of change, the EVM applies it, and the stateRoot is the cryptographic fingerprint of the new world state.

Let's summarize the core concepts from this chapter so they stick. First, the Ethereum Virtual Machine is the deterministic, sandboxed runtime that runs contract bytecode and produces state transitions. Second, the account-based model tracks a global world state mapping addresses to account objects, which differs fundamentally from UTXO systems. Third, the world state is captured compactly by the stateRoot in each block header, permitting cryptographic verification of the full network state. Each of these ideas is practical: the EVM explains why contracts must be written for deterministic behavior, the account model shapes how you design persistent data, and the stateRoot is what nodes compare to ensure consensus. Reflect on how these three ideas connect: the EVM executes code that mutates the world state, and the stateRoot proves the result. Keep these three concepts handy as mental anchors when reading blocks or designing contracts.

Finish with three practical reminders to carry into your development work. First, always check whether a contract account expects a payable transfer before sending native Ether; contracts don't initiate transactions so they need appropriate functions to accept funds. Second, use web3. js to read the block header fields transactionsRoot, stateRoot, and receiptsRoot to validate inclusion and observe post-transaction state; this helps you debug and reason about contract effects. Third, remember that Merkle roots are commitments, not content: you need proofs or the underlying data to reconstruct or verify specific items. These checks help avoid common pitfalls — stuck funds, mistaken assumptions about state, and blind trust in snapshot values. Final takeaway: combine conceptual knowledge with these practical checks to make safer, more reliable dApps.
